# What the assistant should do about Ryan Whitaker's absence

## The short answer

**Leave the code as SC, add a detailed free-text note explaining what actually happened, email the HR Manager before the end of the day, and submit the list before 12:00. Do not change the code to UA.**

## Why not UA?

UA is technically the "catch-all" code – *any other absence that was not booked in advance* – and Ryan's absence doesn't cleanly fit SC, DEP, or BRV. So on a narrow reading of the definitions, UA is the "correct" code. But the assistant must look at what coding it UA will actually do, not just what the dictionary says.

A second UA on someone in probation triggers the payroll system to generate a termination letter that is **sent the same day, at 12:00, with no human in the loop**. The HR Manager is not in today. No one will see that letter before it reaches Ryan. The assistant would be the person who, by choosing a code, sets the machine in motion.

That outcome would be manifestly wrong, for two reasons:

1. **Ryan did exactly what his contract asks of him.** The probation clause exists to make sure new starters "turn up reliably and tell their team leader when they can't." Ryan rang Gary at 05:40 for a 06:00 shift. He communicated before the shift, not after, not at all.
2. **The absence had a genuine, unforeseeable cause.** His sister went into labour two weeks early, her husband was offshore and physically unable to get back, their mother is in Aberdeen. Ryan is her emergency contact. He drove her to Pinderfields and stayed the night. Neither he nor anyone else could have booked this in advance, or avoided it.

Coding it UA and letting the system terminate a man who rang in on time, for the birth of his niece, in the last week of his probation, is not the rule working as intended. It is a gap in the rule being applied in a way that produces a result no reasonable person in the HR function would endorse.

## Why not DEP?

DEP is defined as emergency time off for the employee's *spouse or partner, child or parent, or someone who lives in the employee's household*. Ryan's sister lives in Castleford; he lives alone. She is none of those things. Changing the code to DEP would be misapplying a defined category to make the facts fit, and the assistant's role is to code accurately, not to find the most convenient category.

## Why not BRV?

A birth is not a death. Obvious, but worth stating so the reasoning is complete.

## Why leave it as SC, then, when Ryan wasn't ill?

Because it is the least-wrong code available. It is factually inaccurate – Ryan was not sick – but it is the only code that (a) does not misapply a tighter definition, and (b) does not trigger automatic termination. The practical consequence of SC in his first six months is that the day is unpaid, which is not ideal, but it is a pay issue that the HR Manager can review and correct, not an employment-status issue that cannot be undone.

The inaccuracy is handled transparently by the note, not by papering over it.

## The free-text note

The assistant should write a clear, factual note on the entry, for example:

> **Note added by HR assistant, 6 Nov, 11:50.** Code SC used by team leader; Ryan was not in fact unwell. Per his email of 09:12 today: his sister (his emergency contact) went into labour Wednesday night, approx. two weeks early. Her husband works offshore and was unable to return. Their mother lives in Aberdeen. Ryan drove his sister to Pinderfields Hospital and stayed with her overnight; the baby was born 06:10 Thursday. Ryan rang Gary at 05:40 to say he would not make his 06:00 shift. No available code (DEP, BRV) accurately covers an emergency involving a sibling who does not live in the employee's household. SC retained as the closest available category and to avoid triggering the probation UA count in error. Flagged for HR Manager review.

This keeps the record honest, explains the code choice, and creates a paper trail.

## Email the HR Manager today

Even though she is not in, the assistant should email her with:

- A summary of what happened and the code issue.
- Ryan's own email, forwarded.
- A note that he is one week from the end of probation (12 November) and that this was deliberately not coded UA.
- A recommendation that she (a) review whether the day should be paid rather than treated as an unpaid SC day, and (b) add a short note to Ryan's file recording that the 5 November absence was a family emergency, not sickness and not unauthorised, so that it does not create ambiguity later.
- A flag that the absence categories may need a review, since a family emergency involving a sibling, parent's partner, or other close family member currently has no dedicated code and risks being miscoded as UA.

## Email Ryan

A short, human message acknowledging his email, wishing his sister and the baby well, and confirming that his absence has been noted and is being handled. He has already apologised and shown he understands the probation context; a cold silence from HR on the morning of his niece's birth would be the wrong note to end on, and a brief acknowledgement is low-cost and appropriate.

## Submit the list before 12:00

The payroll run is automatic and uses the list as it stands at 12:00. The assistant has twenty minutes. The list should be submitted on time with Ryan's entry as SC-plus-note, so that payroll is not delayed and no one is left in limbo. Everything else – pay correction, file note, category review – is for the HR Manager on Monday.

## The underlying point

The system was built for the ordinary cases. Ryan's situation – a genuine, communicated, unavoidable family emergency involving a relative who falls outside the narrow DEP definition – exposes a gap. The right thing is not to force his absence into a category that wasn't designed for it, and it is not to let an automated process terminate him for the gap. The right thing is to code as accurately and harmlessly as the available options allow, document the truth plainly, and put the judgment call in front of the person who actually has the authority and the full context to make it.
